sections.hypothesis: Crypto returns show time-series momentum: when BTC or ETH is above where it was 20, 60 and 120 days ago, its following returns are better on average than when it isn't. Holding each market only in proportion to how many of those trends agree, sized down when volatility is above 50% a year, gives a higher Sharpe than buy-and-hold with at most half its maximum drawdown, after costs.
sections.rationale: Time-series momentum is one of the most replicated effects in finance, across futures in every asset class (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen, 2012), and has been found in crypto (Liu and Tsyvinski, 2021). Proposed causes: slow diffusion of information, under-reaction then herding, and trend-chasing flows, all plausible in a retail-heavy market. Volatility targeting rests on a separate finding: volatility clusters and persists, but returns don't rise in proportion, so cutting size in wild periods improves risk-adjusted returns (Moreira and Muir, 2017). Weak points: the crypto evidence comes mostly from one long bull market; trends whipsaw in ranges; a widely known effect may have decayed. This is the idea with the strongest prior evidence in the backlog, which is why it is tested with a strict bar.
sections.rules: Daily bars (1d, each closing at 00:00 UTC). At each close, for each lookback L in 20, 60 and 120 days, a vote is 1 if the close is above the close L days earlier, else 0. Trend = average of the three votes (0, 1/3, 2/3 or 1). Volatility = standard deviation of daily log returns over the last 30 days x sqrt(365). Target weight = trend x min(1, 50% / volatility). Cash until 120 days of history. Decide at the close, trade at the next open; rebalance only when the target differs from the current weight by more than the 2% no-trade band in kestrel.toml. Long only, spot, never above fully invested. BTC and ETH are each run on their own.
sections.falsification: BTCUSDT 1d and ETHUSDT 1d, 2020-01 to 2025-10 (before the holdout), default parameters, run once each. Reject unless, on BOTH markets: (1) Sharpe is above buy-and-hold's Sharpe; (2) max drawdown is no worse than half of buy-and-hold's; (3) total return beats the same market held at the strategy's average exposure (Statistics tab, 'held at the same exposure'), so timing adds something beyond simply holding less; (4) break-even cost is at least twice the cost actually paid; (5) at least 30 orders. Making less money than buy-and-hold is not a rejection: a long-only strategy in cash part of the time will usually trail holding in a bull market, and that is the trade being tested.
sections.parameters: fast_days 20, mid_days 60, slow_days 120, vol_days 30, target_vol_pct 50. The three lookbacks are averaged so no single lookback is chosen. Only the defaults are pre-registered; any other value is a new trial and belongs in P3's walk-forward.
sections.costs: Votes change a few times a year and the 2% band absorbs most daily volatility drift, so expect roughly 20-60 orders a year per market and turnover of about 3-6x equity a year. At about 11 bps per side that is a cost drag near 0.3-0.7% a year: small against the edge claimed. The no-trade band's skips are reported on the Costs and fills tab.
